answers.summary: No public ranking of Ventura County apartment owners by unit count exists. The biggest identifiable private owners come from recent large deals: FPA Multifamily (about 800 units in the Conejo Valley), AEW, Kennedy Wilson, Raintree, Hines and BlackRock. Public housing authorities and nonprofit affordable housing developers also hold large portfolios.
answers.answer:
### Institutional and private owners identified from reported deals
| Owner | Ventura County holdings (reported) | City |
|---|---|---|
| FPA Multifamily | 399 units (Los Robles + Retreat, $171.3M, Dec 2023) + 409 units (Oakview + Biltmore, $153M, Feb 2024), about 808 units. IPA said these portfolios were about 10%-11% of the market-rate stock in Thousand Oaks/Westlake | Thousand Oaks, Westlake Village |
| AEW Capital Management | Ranch at Moorpark, 376 units ($133.2M, Apr 2024) | Moorpark |
| Kennedy Wilson | 386-unit community bought from CSUCI (2016), plus 310 market-rate units planned on a CSUCI ground lease | Camarillo |
| Raintree Partners | Cypress Point, 268 units ($100M, Aug 2025) | Ventura |
| Hines-led venture | Tempo at RiverPark, 235 units ($105M, Jan 2026) | Oxnard |
| Afton | The Landing at Arroyo, 212 units ($95M, Aug 2024) | Simi Valley |
| Jackson Square Properties | Allure at Camarillo, 165 units ($69.5M, Mar 2026) | Camarillo |
| BlackRock-managed account | Santal, 142 units (~$83M, Oct 2025) | Thousand Oaks |

Matthews estimates that **institutional and REIT buyers accounted for about 30% of acquisition volume** over the past five years. The other roughly 70% is private: families, syndicators and local operators.

### Other large owner categories to map
- **Public housing authorities** in the county's larger cities, which own and operate public and affordable units.
- **Nonprofit affordable developers** active in the county.
- **Public apartment REITs**, which have historically owned Ventura County communities. Confirm current holdings in their 10-K property schedules.

### How to build the real list
1. In CoStar, run Owners for Ventura County multifamily and sort by units owned. Export each owner's portfolio.
2. Cross-check against assessor parcel data for owner names and mailing addresses, using a data tool such as CoStar, Reonomy or PropertyRadar.
3. Roll LLCs up to their parents. Many owners hold each asset in a separate LLC, so group by mailing address and by signatory on recorded deeds.

### So what
The top 20 owners are institutions you approach through their asset managers. Your listing pipeline is the next 200 owners: private families with 2-10 buildings each.

answers.summary: Institutional owners in Ventura County typically hold 5-10 years. Private family owners often hold 20-35+ years. Recent sellers show the range, from Alturas (about 3 years) to Cypress Point's original developer (35 years).
answers.answer:
### Hold periods visible in recent deals
| Property | Seller | Bought | Sold | Hold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cypress Point, Ventura | County Center LP (original developer) | 1990 | 2025 | ~35 yrs |
| Ranch at Moorpark | Decron Properties | 2013 ($84.4M) | 2024 ($133.2M) | ~11 yrs |
| Tempo at RiverPark, Oxnard | Bascom venture | 2018 ($75.25M) | 2026 ($105M) | ~8 yrs |
| Allure at Camarillo | Nuveen | ~2018 | 2026 | ~8 yrs |
| Vines at RiverPark, Oxnard | Champion Real Estate | 2016 | 2022 | ~6 yrs |
| Alturas, Oxnard | FPA Multifamily | 2018 ($34M) | 2021 ($50.7M) | ~3 yrs |

### By owner type (working ranges, estimated)
- **Value-add funds and syndicators:** 3-7 years, driven by fund life and the business plan. Alturas and the Vines are examples.
- **Core and core-plus institutions:** 7-12 years. Examples are Nuveen, Bascom and Decron.
- **Private families and original developers:** 20-40 years, often until death or a generational transition. Prop 13 makes long holds cheap: the tax base stays low, and the step-up in basis at death wipes out embedded capital gains.

### What this means for timing
- **Institutional owners:** watch fund vintages and acquisition dates. Assets bought in 2016-2019 are now 7-10 years in and likely sale candidates. Tempo and Allure both sold on that timeline.
- **Private owners:** the trigger is life events, not the calendar. Death, divorce, retirement, a partner dispute, or a loan maturity.
- **Recent volume tells you about future listings.** Buildings that traded in the 2021-2022 peak and carry floating or short-term debt are the most likely forced or early sellers.

### So what
- **Sort your owner database by last sale date.** Anything held 20+ years by an individual or family trust gets an estate- and tax-aware conversation (Q97-Q99).
- **Anything bought by a fund 6-10 years ago** gets a broker opinion of value (BOV) pitch to the asset manager.
keyPoints: Institutional holds: typically ~5-10 years (Tempo ~8, Allure ~8, Ranch at Moorpark ~11)
Private family and developer holds: often 20-35+ years (Cypress Point: 35)
Value-add funds: ~3-7 years (Alturas ~3, Vines ~6)
Prop 13 and the step-up in basis at death encourage very long private holds
Prospect funds 6-10 years into a hold; prospect families on life events

answers.summary: No one publishes this number for Ventura County apartments. Based on how long private owners hold, a reasonable working estimate is that 40%-60% of small (2-20 unit) buildings have had the same owner for 20+ years and carry a Prop 13 tax base far below market. You can measure it yourself from assessor transfer dates.
answers.answer:
### Why the share is high here
- **Prop 13** limits assessed-value growth to **2% a year** until a change in ownership. Anyone who bought before about 2006 has a tax base that is a fraction of today's value.
- **Since Prop 19 (effective Feb 16, 2021),** the parent-child reassessment exclusion applies **only to a family home or family farm**, not to rental property. Heirs who inherit apartments are reassessed to market value. That pushes families toward selling, or toward careful entity planning, at transfer.
- **Large institutional assets turn over every 5-10 years** (see Q96), so the long-hold, low-basis owners sit mostly in the **2-50 unit segment**. The densest concentrations are in older parts of Oxnard, Ventura (midtown and westside), Santa Paula, Port Hueneme and Simi Valley.

### Estimate (working, low confidence)
| Segment | Share held 20+ years (est.) |
|---|---|
| 2-4 units | 35%-50% |
| 5-20 units | 40%-60% |
| 100+ units | Under 15% |

### How to measure it precisely
1. Pull assessor parcel data for all multifamily land-use codes, from a data vendor or the Ventura County Assessor.
2. Use the **last transfer date** (or base year) as a proxy. Filter for transfers before 2006.
3. Compare **assessed value vs. estimated market value.** A ratio below 0.35 signals a deeply embedded Prop 13 base.
4. Exclude institutional owners. Flag individual and trust owners (look for names ending in "Trust," "TR," "Family Trust").

### So what
These owners have a **low tax basis and large embedded capital gains.** Selling triggers both a large tax bill and, for the buyer, a property tax reset to about 1.1% of the price. Your pitch is a tax plan, not a price: a 1031 into a management-free asset (NNN or a DST), an installment sale, or holding until death for the step-up if that fits their estate plan.
keyPoints: Prop 13: assessed value grows at most 2% a year until a change in ownership
Prop 19 (Feb 16, 2021): parent-child exclusion limited to the family home or farm, so rentals reassess at transfer
Working estimate: ~40%-60% of 5-20 unit buildings held 20+ years (estimate)
Measure it from assessor last-transfer dates and the assessed-to-market value ratio
Pitch to low-basis owners: a tax and estate solution, such as a 1031, DST or installment sale

answers.summary: Ventura County skews older: median age is 40.2. Among owner-occupied households, 37.6% are headed by someone 65 or older, and 17.4% by someone 75 or older (ACS 2024). Apartment owners skew older still. Expect a large share of private multifamily owners to face estate or succession decisions within 10 years.
answers.answer:
### Demographic proxies (ACS 2024 1-year, Ventura County)
| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Population | 835,427 |
| Median age | 40.2 (California: 38.4) |
| Population 65+ | ~155,200 (18.6%) |
| Owner-occupied households | 186,668 |
| Owner households headed by 65+ | 70,192 (37.6%) |
| Owner households headed by 75+ | 32,445 (17.4%) |

Source: Census table B25007, tenure by age of householder.

### Translating that to apartment owners (estimate)
These figures cover homeowners, not apartment owners. But individual and trust owners of small apartment buildings are typically older than homeowners overall, because they built the portfolio over decades. A reasonable working assumption is that **40%-50% of individually held 2-20 unit buildings are controlled by someone 65+**. That works out to **thousands of buildings countywide** facing succession within 10-15 years.

### Why this matters more after Prop 19
- **Rental property loses the parent-child reassessment exclusion,** so heirs inherit a property tax reset to market value.
- **Heirs often don't want to manage.** Siblings disagree, and many live outside the county.
- **The step-up in basis at death** means heirs can often sell with little capital gains tax. That makes **post-death sales very common.**

### How to find them
1. From assessor or vendor data, filter individual and trust owners with a **last transfer date before 2000**.
2. Append age data through a skip-trace or data vendor, where legally permitted.
3. Watch **probate filings** at Ventura County Superior Court, and recorded **affidavits of death of trustee** at the County Recorder.
4. Build CPA, estate attorney and trust officer referral relationships.

### So what
Succession is your biggest single source of listings. Lead with education: Prop 19, step-up in basis, 1031, DSTs. Leave the pricing pitch for later.
keyPoints: Median age 40.2; 18.6% of residents are 65+ (ACS 2024)
37.6% of owner-occupied households are headed by someone 65+, 17.4% by 75+
Working estimate: ~40%-50% of individually held 2-20 unit buildings controlled by someone 65+
Prop 19 removes parent-child reassessment relief for rentals
Signals: probate filings and recorded affidavits of death of trustee

answers.summary: Many small and mid-size Ventura County apartment buildings are held in revocable living trusts. Owner names like "Smith Family Trust" or "TR" are visible on assessor and recorded documents. Trustee and heir identities are private, so find them through recorded documents and probate filings rather than a published list.
answers.answer:
### What's public and what isn't
- **Public:** the vesting name on the deed and assessor roll (e.g., "John and Mary Doe, Trustees of the Doe Family Trust dated 3/1/1998"), the mailing address, recorded trust transfer deeds, affidavits of death of trustee, and probate filings if a court case is opened.
- **Not public:** the trust instrument itself, the beneficiaries, and successor trustees, unless they are named in a recorded document or court filing.

We are deliberately not naming private individuals here. The method below is how to identify them yourself, ethically.

### Research method
1. **Filter the owner file.** In assessor or vendor data (CoStar, PropertyRadar, Reonomy), filter multifamily parcels where the owner name contains "TRUST," "TR," "TTEE," "SURVIVOR'S TRUST" or "BYPASS TRUST."
2. **Read the vesting deed** from the Ventura County Recorder index. It names the trustees at the time of the deed.
3. **Look for succession signals:**
   - an *affidavit of death of trustee* (names the successor trustee)
   - a trustee's deed transferring to beneficiaries
   - a change of mailing address to a CPA or attorney's office
   - a **sub-trust name** such as "Survivor's Trust" or "Exemption Trust," which usually means one spouse has died
4. **Check probate.** Ventura County Superior Court probate filings show estates where the property was not in a trust.
5. **Contact the right way.** Send a mailed letter to the trustee at the record address, and work through the family's CPA or estate attorney when they are known. Follow do-not-call and privacy rules, and be sensitive to timing after a death.

### Why trusts matter
- **Successor trustees** have a fiduciary duty to beneficiaries. They want a defensible process: a broker opinion of value (BOV), multiple bids, and documented marketing.
- **Several beneficiaries** often want cash, which favors a sale over continued management.
- **Prop 19 reassessment** on transfer to children who don't live in the property increases the pressure to sell.

### So what
- **Offer a free BOV and a "trustee's guide to selling"** covering the Prop 19 reassessment, step-up in basis, a 1031 for beneficiaries who want to stay invested, and a timeline.
- **Trustees hire the broker who makes the process defensible.**
keyPoints: Vesting names ("Trustee of the ___ Trust") are public; beneficiaries usually aren't
Signals: affidavit of death of trustee, sub-trust names (Survivor's/Bypass), mailing address moved to a CPA or attorney
Sources: assessor owner file, County Recorder index, Superior Court probate
Successor trustees want a defensible process: BOV, competitive bids, documentation
Do not compile or publish heir lists. Contact trustees respectfully at the record address

answers.summary: Today's sellers are mostly driven by life events and fatigue, not price peaks. The main motivators are aging owners and estate planning, management and regulatory fatigue, rising insurance and operating costs, loan maturities on 2019-2022 debt, and institutional fund exits.
answers.answer:
### The main motivators (roughly in order of frequency for private owners, our judgment)
1. **Estate and succession.** An aging owner base (37.6% of owner households are headed by someone 65+, per ACS 2024). Prop 19 reassesses rentals on transfer to children, and heirs prefer cash or a 1031 into passive assets.
2. **Regulatory fatigue.** AB 1482 caps increases at 5% + CPI (max 10%) and requires just cause. SB 567 (2024) tightened owner-move-in and remodel evictions. SB 721 balcony inspections, and city-level rules, add more. Small owners feel this most.
3. **Operating costs.** Insurance premiums and availability, utilities, repairs and payroll are growing faster than the roughly 1% rent growth (Matthews H1 2026, +1.2% year over year).
4. **Debt.** Loans originated in 2019-2022 at 3%-4% are maturing into a **5.5%-6.25%** permanent rate environment (Colliers, mid-2026). A refinance may require a cash-in paydown.
5. **Fund life cycles.** Institutions sell on schedule: Bascom (8 years, Tempo), Nuveen (8 years, Allure), Latigo (merchant build, Santal).
6. **Opportunity and rebalancing.** Owners use a 1031 to trade management-heavy apartments for NNN, DSTs or out-of-state assets with lower regulation.

### What is NOT driving sales
- **Peak pricing.** Caps are about 120 bps wider than in 2022 (Matthews). Sellers who don't have to sell mostly wait.

### Reading the signals
| Signal | Likely motivation |
|---|---|
| Owner 70+, trust-held, bought before 2000 | Estate / succession |
| Recent rent-board or code complaints, deferred maintenance | Fatigue |
| Loan recorded 2016-2021 on a 5-7 year term | Maturity |
| Fund-owned, bought 2016-2019 | Fund exit |
| Owner lives out of state | Fatigue / rebalancing |

### So what
- **Tailor the first conversation to the motivation.** Lead with estate and tax education for heirs, a refinance-vs-sell analysis for maturities, and a 1031 path for fatigue.
- **Rate-driven urgency is real** for leveraged owners, but rare among free-and-clear long-term holders.
keyPoints: Top private-owner drivers: estate/succession, regulatory fatigue, rising costs
Debt: 2019-2022 loans at 3%-4% maturing into 5.5%-6.25% perm rates (Colliers, mid-2026)
Rent growth about +1.2% YoY (Matthews H1 2026) lags expense growth
Institutional sellers exit on 6-10 year fund cycles (Tempo, Allure)
Price peaks are not a driver: caps are ~120 bps above 2022

answers.summary: There is no public list of loans maturing in the next 24 months. You build one from recorded deeds of trust and loan data in CoStar or other vendors. Focus on 5- to 10-year loans originated in 2016-2021, plus bridge loans from 2021-2024. We don't name private borrowers here.
answers.answer:
### Who is most exposed (by loan type)
| Loan vintage / type | Typical term | Matures | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agency or bank 5-yr fixed, 2021-2022 | 5 yrs | 2026-2027 | High: coupon jumps from ~3% to ~6% |
| 7-yr fixed, 2019-2020 | 7 yrs | 2026-2027 | High |
| 10-yr fixed, 2016-2018 | 10 yrs | 2026-2028 | Medium: appreciation since origination often covers it |
| Bridge or floating, 2021-2024 | 2-3 yrs + extensions | 2025-2028 | Highest: rate caps expire and debt service coverage is thin |

**Public example of a recent bridge loan:** Jackson Square's 2026 Allure at Camarillo purchase was funded with a **bridge loan of about $46.75M from M&T Realty Capital** (per Traded and The Registry). Bridge loans like this typically mature in a few years, which is a future refinance-or-sell event.

Not all maturities create distress. Bascom refinanced Tempo with a $47M New York Life loan in 2018 and still sold in 2026 at a large gain ($75.25M bought vs. $105M sold).

### How to build the list
1. **CoStar or Reonomy loan data:** filter Ventura County multifamily by **estimated maturity date** between now and 2028, with lender and original amount.
2. **County Recorder:** search deeds of trust by APN or grantor and record date. Infer the term from lender type. Banks and credit unions usually lend 5-7 years; Fannie and Freddie 5-10.
3. **CMBS and agency loans:** use Trepp or the Freddie/Fannie loan-level disclosures for larger assets.
4. **Prioritize:** a high loan-to-current-value ratio, debt service coverage near 1.0x at today's rates, and an owner with few other assets.

### Outreach angle
Don't open with "your loan is maturing." Offer a **refinance-vs-sell analysis**:
- the new loan size at a 1.25x DSCR and 6% rate
- the cash-in required
- the net proceeds from selling now

Partner with a mortgage broker so the advice is credible.

### So what
In a 5.5%-6.25% debt market, maturities are one of the few events that force a decision on a set date. Track them 12-18 months ahead.
keyPoints: No public maturity list exists. Use CoStar or Reonomy loan data plus Recorder deeds of trust
Highest-risk loans: 2021-2022 five-year fixed and 2021-2024 bridge or floating debt
Example: Allure at Camarillo bought in 2026 with a ~$46.75M M&T bridge loan
Permanent debt is at 5.5%-6.25% vs. ~3%-4% on 2020-2021 loans
Pitch a refinance-vs-sell analysis 12-18 months before maturity

answers.summary: No single list of distressed apartments exists. You build one from recorded notices of default and trustee sales, city code enforcement records, unlawful-detainer and receivership court filings, and visible deferred maintenance. Overall distress is low because owners have equity and occupancy is about 96%.
answers.answer:
### Context: distress is limited
- **Fundamentals are solid.** CBRE puts occupancy at **96.1%** in Q2 2026, and most long-term owners have large equity cushions.
- **Distress is concentrated in three places:**
  1. Buildings bought at **2021-2022 peak pricing with short-term or floating debt**
  2. **Older buildings with deferred maintenance,** where insurance, SB 721 balcony findings or code orders force capital spending
  3. **Small owners squeezed** by AB 1482 caps and expense growth

### Where to find it (research method)
| Signal | Source |
|---|---|
| Notice of default (NOD), notice of trustee sale (NTS) | Ventura County Recorder; foreclosure data vendors (PropertyRadar, ATTOM) |
| Code enforcement cases, red/yellow tags, substandard housing | City code enforcement departments (Oxnard, Ventura, Simi Valley, Thousand Oaks, etc.) via public records requests or online portals |
| Receiverships, unlawful-detainer volume, partnership disputes | Ventura County Superior Court case search |
| Tax delinquency | Ventura County Treasurer-Tax Collector defaulted-tax records |
| Deferred maintenance | Drive-bys, Google Street View, tenant reviews, long-vacant units on rental sites |
| Lis pendens, mechanic's liens | County Recorder |

### Prioritize
1. An NOD or tax delinquency on a 5+ unit building
2. Open code cases plus an older vintage (pre-1980)
3. An owner who bought in 2021-2022 with a high loan-to-value ratio

### Approach
- **Distressed owners need options,** not judgment. Offer a quick, discreet BOV, a buyer list of value-add and all-cash 1031 buyers, and lender negotiation support through a partner.
- **Follow the rules.** California foreclosure-consultant law and the related rules on distressed residential properties may limit some solicitations. Check with counsel before any outreach that offers help avoiding foreclosure.

### So what
- **Expect a handful of true distress situations a year,** not a wave.
- **Deferred maintenance is far more common than default.** It is the value-add buyer's favorite product.

### How to build each city's top-owner list
1. **CoStar Owners report**, filtered by city and multifamily, ranked by units. Roll up LLCs to the parent entity.
2. **Assessor parcel data** (through a vendor) for owner names and mailing addresses on 2-50 unit parcels, which CoStar covers less completely.
3. **Recorded deeds** to identify signatories and managers of LLCs.

### How to reach them
- **Institutions:** find the asset manager or acquisitions lead through LinkedIn and press releases. Pitch market data, BOVs and buyer intelligence. They respond to brokers who bring deals and comps.
- **Private owners:**
  1. Mail a personalized letter with a one-page market update
  2. Follow up by phone, after scrubbing against do-not-call lists
  3. Ask property managers in each city for introductions
  4. Run CPA and estate-attorney referral programs
  5. Host an owner seminar on Prop 19, 1031 exchanges and AB 1482
- **CRM discipline:** tag each owner by city, unit count, hold length, trust status and loan maturity, and contact them quarterly.

### So what
- **Pick one city to own first.** Oxnard has the most units, with CBRE showing about 13,300 in its tracked inventory. Ventura has about 10,800.
- **Become the broker who knows every 5+ unit owner there** within 90 days.

answers.summary: Seller objections fall into six groups: price ("I'll wait for 2021 values"), taxes ("the capital gains will kill me"), timing ("rates will drop"), loyalty ("I don't want to hurt my tenants"), "I don't know what I'd do with the money," and "I'll just sell it myself." Answer each with numbers and a plan, not pressure.
answers.answer:
### Common objections and how to answer them
1. **"I'll wait until prices come back to 2021-22."**
   Caps averaged **4.19% in 2022 vs. 5.37% in H1 2026** (Matthews). Getting back requires rates to fall a lot. Meanwhile rent growth is about 1% while expenses rise. Show them their NOI at both cap rates, and what waiting three years actually earns.

2. **"The capital gains tax will kill me."**
   There are several tools:
   - a **1031 exchange** into NNN, a DST or a lower-management asset
   - an **installment sale**
   - a **721 UPREIT** contribution
   - or hold until death for the **step-up in basis**

   Bring in their CPA early. The question is net after tax, not gross price.

3. **"Rates will drop and buyers will pay more."**
   Possibly. But with the 10-year Treasury at about 4.4%-4.7% and permanent debt at **5.5%-6.25%** (mid-2026), even a 50 bp drop moves caps only modestly. Supply is low (502 units under construction), so well-priced buildings are trading now: Tempo $105M, Allure $69.5M.

4. **"My tenants have been with me 20 years. I don't want them displaced."**
   AB 1482 caps increases and requires just cause, and SB 567 limits renovation evictions. A buyer can't simply clear the building. We can target long-hold buyers and include tenant-friendly terms.

5. **"I'd just have to reinvest. What would I even buy?"**
   Set up the replacement plan before listing: DST menus, NNN properties, or a larger building with professional management. Then the sale is an upgrade, not an exit.

6. **"Your commission is too high. I'll sell to someone who called me."**
   Unsolicited buyers usually offer below market. Closings ran about **94% of original list** in the MLS data, and competitive processes like Tempo and Allure drew institutional bids. Show the net difference.

7. **"Prop 13. My taxes are so low."**
   That benefit ends for the next owner anyway. Prop 19 reassesses rental property when it passes to the children. Plan the exit on your terms.

### So what
Most objections are really fear of the tax bill or the unknown. Lead with a written **net-proceeds and reinvestment plan**.
keyPoints: Price: caps averaged 4.19% (2022) vs. 5.37% (H1 2026). Show the NOI math
Tax: 1031, DST, installment sale, 721 UPREIT, or hold for step-up. Involve the CPA
Rates: perm debt 5.5%-6.25%; a 50 bp drop moves caps only modestly
Tenants: AB 1482 and SB 567 protect long-term residents
Prop 13 objection: Prop 19 reassesses rentals passed to children anyway
